text: I don't think people really understand exam pressure until they go through it. It sounds like someone wailing about some useless nonsense, until you realise it's an actual, real thing. And people react to it in different ways. I used to be the 'give up and stare at the clock' person, like literally. But now? Now, when I start to get consumed by doubts and negative thoughts like, 'you're gonna fail your GCSEs', 'you're cooked ', 'this question is a 5 marker... you can't do this,' 'I'm doomed', 'I didn't revise properly', 'why are there so many 5 markers?!!', 'I need to read the question for the 4th time', 'I'm losing time', 'I have 5 minutes',' I didn't recheck my answers', 'the answers not C, it's A', 'change it to A', 'what if it's C?', 'I'll lose a mark because I'm stupid'......... I just stop. I stop writing, I stop thinking, I close the paper. And I just sit there for a good 5 minutes, and breathe. Deep breaths. And it actually works. It clears me out and I suddenly realise, it's not the end of the world. I don't need Grade 9s and 8s, that's what I would LIKE, but not what I need. I need a good Grade 5, and even a grade 4, it's a pass, isn't it? If you're not good at a subject, and you know you're not good at it, don't beg for a grade 9 just work hard for a pass. That's it, and that's a lot. People need to understand that getting a Grade 9 for every single subject is extremely unrealistic. If you get grade 7 and 6s, be proud, because that's hard to get. And just work hard, so you don't think back and wish you'd tried harder, cause I'm telling you, the only reason people fail, is because they give up. 'Believe in yourself, and you're already halfway there' If you have exams, good luck, YOU'LL DO WELL

text: Small summary 7 Tips To Beat Exam Anxiety 1. Sleep is crucial to get at least 6 hours no allnighters 2. Have a balanced diet at least one week prior to exam date breakfast high in complex carbohydrates and fibre on exam day 3. Practice positive selfimagery. Be practical with this or it WILL NOT WORK. 4. Try to picture yourself in a happy moment and then QUICKLY switch to imagining yourself in the exam room. Associates happy feeling with your exam and primes you to be ready. 5. Before the exam try to picture exam questions you have already studied to BOOST your confidence. 6. Important you familiarise yourself with the exam room which makes you feel more at ease on the day of the exam. 7. Write down insecurities on a paper and crumple the paper and chuck it away. Keep a reminder to observe your breath sensations throughout the day and night at home, during studies, exams, when travelling etc with eyes open or closed. text: The physiological sigh that Huberman talks about is something I use constantly in my facilitation work. Two short inhales through the nose followed by an extended exhale through the mouth. It works because the double inhale pops open the alveoli in your lungs that have collapsed, maximizing surface area for gas exchange. The long exhale then activates the parasympathetic nervous system through the vagus nerve. What I find in practice is that combining this with cold exposure creates a much deeper training effect. When someone is sitting in 3 degree water and their body is in full sympathetic activation, using breath control to deliberately shift into calm is the most powerful stress inoculation I have seen. The skill transfers directly to high pressure situations outside the water. After six years of running these sessions I still find it remarkable how fast people can shift their state once they understand the mechanism.

text: Key Insights on Managing Stress Anxiety A Neuroscientific Perspective Based on the Huberman Lab Essentials Episode 1. Stress as a BrainBody Phenomenon Stress Defined Stress is a generalized system mobilizing brain and body resources when internal experiences clash with external demands. It involves the sympathetic nervous system activation and parasympathetic nervous system calming. Neurological Basis The sympathetic chain ganglia neurons along the spine release epinephrine adrenaline, priming the body for action e.g., increased heart rate, blood flow to muscles. Conversely, the parasympathetic system slows bodily functions e.g., digestion during stress. 2. Tools for Immediate Stress Relief The Physiological Sigh Mechanism A rapid breathing technique to counteract acute stress Double inhale through the nose Long exhale through the mouth. Why It Works Reinflates collapsed lung alveoli, expels excess CO, and triggers the parasympathetic nervous system to lower heart rate. Effectiveness Reduces stress within 2030 seconds. Repeat 13 times as needed. 3. ShortTerm Stress Benefits Immune Activation Positive Role Acute stress enhances immune function by releasing adrenaline, which mobilizes infectionfighting cells e.g., from the spleen. Tool Cyclic Hyperventilation Wim Hof Method Protocol 2530 rapid inhalesexhales Hold breath for 1530 seconds postexhale. Repeat 23 cycles. Outcome Boosts adrenaline, combats infections, and reduces inflammatory responses supported by studies on endotoxin tolerance. Caution Avoid breathholding near water consult a doctor for preexisting conditions. 4. MediumTerm Stress Raising Stress Threshold Stress Inoculation Deliberately exposing oneself to stressors e.g., cold showers, intense exercise to build tolerance. Tool Cognitive Calming Under Activation Panoramic Vision Widen gaze avoid tunnel vision during high stress to activate brainstem circuits that reduce mental agitation. Practice During physical exertion e.g., sprinting, consciously relax the mind while the body remains activated. 5. LongTerm Stress Mitigating Chronic Damage Key Risks Chronic stress erodes brain structures e.g., hippocampus, weakens immunity, and increases cardiovascular risks. Critical Tools Social Connection Activates serotonin linked to wellbeing and neural repair. Prioritize trusted relationships, pets, or activities that spark delight. Supplements Use Judiciously Ashwagandha Lowers cortisol and anxiety shortterm use recommended. LTheanine 100200 mg Enhances relaxation and sleep quality via GABA modulation. Avoid HighDose Melatonin Disrupts hormonal balance prioritize natural lightdark cycles for sleep. 6. Organizational Framework for Emotional Health Three Stress Timescales 1. Acute secondsminutes Use physiological sigh or cyclic breathing. 2. Medium daysweeks Build resilience via stress inoculation. 3. Chronic monthsyears Invest in social bonds, sleep, and antiinflammatory habits. Core Principle Stress is neither inherently good nor badits impact depends on context, duration, and controllability. Conclusion Stress management requires a tailored, sciencebacked approach 1. Leverage Physiology Use breathwork physiological sigh, cyclic breathing to modulate acute stress. 2. Build Resilience Train the mind to stay calm during physical activation e.g., panoramic vision. 3. Prioritize Connection Social bonds and serotonin are foundational for longterm emotional health. 4. Supplement Strategically Ashwagandha and Ltheanine can aid stress modulation but are not substitutes for lifestyle fundamentals. By understanding stress as a dynamic brainbody interplay, we can harness its adaptive power while mitigating harm. The key lies in realtime tools for acute relief, deliberate practice for resilience, and sustained investment in relationships and restorative habits. Stress is not your enemyits a signal. In The Burnout Challenge, she emphasizes 'rethinking burnout' by shifting the weight onto the systemic environment rather than the individual. She famously uses the 'canary in the coal mine' allegory if a canary dies in a toxic mine, we don't try to make the canary more resilient or teach it 'yoga'we fix the mine. While personal coping mechanisms like boundaries and sleep are vital for mental health, focusing solely on 'learning ways to cope' can inadvertently turn wellness into a bandaid. It risks shifting the burden of a systemic issue onto the individual, allowing organizations to avoid addressing the core 'mismatches'like workload or lack of fairnessthat cause the burnout in the first place. Id love to see more discussion on how we can move from individual resilience to organizational accountability!

text: This is what works for me 1. Wake up and get up at the same time every day, even when you are not working. Do not worry about what time you go to bed if you have a few late nights and you get enough fresh air and exercise, you will eventually want to have an early night or two to catch up on your sleep. Sleep is the best thing for stress and anxiety, but worrying about not getting enough is counterproductive, so just go with the flow. 2. Get out into the fresh air and walk. Exercise in the gym is all very well, but nothing beats being outside, even when the weather is cold and wet, you can just wrap up. 3. Try and reduce your coffee intake. Im not good at this, but at least I am trying. 4. Try and analyse your feelings if you are worrying. Find out what is at the bottom of your worries, and write out some possible solutions to them. 5. Use welcome distractions like reading, puzzles, creative pasttimes. 6. Do not drink alcohol when you are stressed or anxious. 7. Sometimes you just have to accept that stress and anxiety is inevitable when you are in certain situations, and in the shortterm, just accept it. Dont fight it or tell yourself that shouldnt feel this way, this is how you feel and pretending otherwise causes problems down the line.

text: The Neuropsychology of relaxation and a novel procedure for sustaining relaxation that it entails Much ink has been spilled on describing the neuropsychology of stress, but very little on the neuropsychology of relaxation, which is surprisingly simple, yet has been overshadowed by its incorrect appellation as a meditative state. Here is an explanation and novel procedure for sustaining relaxation that ironically has little to do with meditation. In a 1984 article in the flagship journal of the APA, The American Psychologist, the psychologist David Holmes reviewed the literature on meditation and concluded that meditative states are no different from resting states. The article linked below was roundly criticized because resting was presumably a dormant and nonaffective state, quite at odds with the fact that meditation has affective and cognitive entailments that go beyond mere resting. However, from the perspective of affective neuroscience, resting states are not simple nonaffective states but are dynamic affective states that are continually modulated by information derived from inner thoughts to outward perceptions. This position is not difficult to understand, and can be summarized below and easily falsified through simple procedure. The ideal for any scientist with a great idea is to be able to explain it in a minute, and to confirm or falsify it as quickly. The world record for this arguably goes to the English philosopher Samuel Johnson, who rejected Archbishop Berkeleys argument that material things only exist in ones mind by striking his foot against a large stone while proclaiming, I refute it thusly! So here is a novel procedure demonstrating the continuity of rest from mindful to flow states, quickly refutable with a good swift kick! Summary Endogenous opioids are induced when we eat, drink, have sex, and relax, and are responsible for our pleasures. Opioid activity however is not static, but labile, or changeable. When elicited, opioid release is always modulated by concurrently perceived novel actoutcome expectancies which may range from negative to positive. If they are negative e.g. a spate of bad news or bad implications of our behavior, opioid activity is suppressed and our pleasures are reduced anhedonia, but if they are positive, then opioid activity is enhanced and our pleasures are accentuated as well peak experience, flow. This is due to dopamineopioid interactions, or the fact that actoutcome discrepancy, or positive or negative surprises, can induce or suppress dopaminergic activity, which in turn can enhance or suppress opioid release. This can be demonstrated procedurally, and if correct, can provide a therapeutic tool to increase arousal and pleasure, or positive wellbeing, and mitigate stress. Basic Facts Endogenous opioids are induced when we eat, drink, have sex, and relax. Their affective correlate, or how it feels, is a sense of pleasure. The neuromodulator dopamine is released upon the anticipation or perception of positive actoutcome discrepancy or novelty, and is felt a sense of arousal or energy, but not pleasure. Fun Fact When we are concurrently perceiving some activity that has a variable and unexpected rate of reward while consuming something pleasurable, opioid activity increases and with it a higher sense of pleasure. In other words, popcorn tastes better when we are watching an exciting movie than when we are watching paint dry. The same effect occurs when we are performing highly variable rewarding or meaningful activity creating art, doing good deeds, doing productive work while in a pleasurable relaxed state. Meaning would be defined as behavior that has branching novel positive implications. This is commonly referred to as flow or peak experience. The same phenomenon underscores the placebo effect, which describes how expectancies can increase dopamine and opioid activity, such as when a meal is tastier or a sugar pill reduces pain when we anticipate they will. So why does this occur? DopamineOpioid interactions or the fact that dopamine activity elicited by positive novel events, and responsible for a state of arousal, but not pleasure interacts with our pleasures as reflected by mid brain opioid systems, and can actually stimulate opioid release, which is reflected in selfreports of greater pleasure. Proof or kicking the stone Just get relaxed using a relaxation protocol such as progressive muscle relaxation, eyes closed rest, or mindfulness, and then follow it by exclusively attending to or performing meaningful activity, and avoiding all meaningless activity or distraction. Keep it up and you will not only stay relaxed, but continue so with a greater sense of wellbeing or pleasure. In other words, this is a procedural bridge between mindful and flow experiences that are not unique psychological states, but merely represent special aspects of resting states. The attribution of affective value to meaningful behavior makes the latter seem autotelic, or reinforcing in itself, and the resultant persistent m to meaning o out the occasions we might have spent dwelling on other meaningless worries and concerns. A Likely Explanation, as if you need one! A more formal explanation from a neurologically based learning theory of this technique is provided on pp. 4451 in a little opensource book on the psychology of rest linked below. The flow experience discussed on pp. 8186. The book is based on the work of the distinguished affective neuroscientist Kent Berridge, who was kind to review for accuracy and endorse the work. From meditation to flow Affect in rest is labile, or changeable, and rest i.e. the general deactivation of the covert musculature is not an inert and nonaffective state, but modulates affective systems in the brain. In addition, the degree of the modulation of pleasurable affect induced by rest is not dependent upon a species of attention focal meditation, mindfulness meditation, but is schedule dependent, and correlates with the variability of schedules or contingencies of reward and the discriminative aspects of incentives i.e. their cognitive implications. In other words, sustained meaningful activity or the anticipation of acting meaningfully during resting states increases the affective tone or value of that behavior, thus making productive work autotelic, or rewarding in itself, and providing a consistent feeling of arousal and pleasure, or shall we say, happiness. text: Nervous System Regulation v. True Healing and Embodiment There is a significant tension in the world of nervous system work between regulation and resolution. Most of what is taught todaybreathwork, cold plunges, or rhythmic tappingis designed to move the needle from a hot, frantic state back to a cool, functional state. This is surface regulation. It is a vital survival skill, but if its used to bypass the pinched sensations of childhood repression, it becomes just another sophisticated way to escape feeling scary stuff. In the landscape of recovery, there are very few exceptions to this rule. However, a few specific approaches attempt to bridge the gap The BottomUp Exceptions The most notable exceptions are found in somatic modalities that refuse to view activation as something to be managed. In these spaces, a heavy chest or a tight throat isn't seen as a symptom to be regulated away, but as the actual doorway. Somatic Experiencing Developed by Peter Levine, this focuses on titrationtaking a tiny drop of the hot repressed energy and letting the body process it without being overwhelmed. It isn't just about getting calm it's about letting the body finally finish a survival reflex that was frozen decades ago. The Kiloby Inquiries This is perhaps the most direct exception. It uses a Reverse Inquiry to intentionally trigger the buried emotion so that it can be looked at. Instead of trying to feel better, the goal is to get better at feeling. By firing consciousness into the center of the contraction, the repression is unmasked rather than just calmed down. The Trap of the Regulated Ego Many people fall into a trap where they become professional regulators. They have the perfect morning routine and the perfect breathing cadence, but their life still feels like a performance. Their nervous system is quiet, but it isn't free. The clench is still there its just been sedated by biohacking. True resolution only happens when the system realizes it no longer needs to repress anything to be safe. You can't regulate your way into that realization. You have to go toward the hot zone, stay with the raw data of the buried emotion, and allow the body to realize that the old threat is over. The only real exception to surface regulation is the willingness to be dysregulated long enough to let the past finally burn off. Join my Third Dimension membership level on YouTube Join this channel

text: This video topic makes me think, so much, about the following quote from 2011 Restoration Therapy Understanding and Guiding Healing in Marriage Family Therapy. In the book, the author, Dr. Terry Hargrave, writes the following Another way that people who protect themselves from perceived lack of safety in relationships through control behaviors is to be performance driven. Typical of this type of performancedriven behavior is the wish by someone to absolutely ensure that that there is no perceived vulnerability in terms of safety. If, for example, the controller determines that he or she could be safe by having a financial savings account of 10,000, he or she would likely work to achieve the goal. But, after the goal was achieved, he or she would discover that the financial vulnerability still existed in other words, the person might have saved 10,000, but they still FEEL unsafeinsecurefinancially vulnerable. He or she would feel driven perhaps to double the amount of money to 20,000. Of course, no matter how much money the controller saved, he or she would still feel vulnerable and then have expectations about how he or she should handle or invest the money. In other words, each step of performance with the money sets the stage for a more complicated and higher performance level. Controllers often find this performance double bind with finances, achievement, education, status, and career, just to name a few areas of struggle. At each new rung of performance achievement, the controller finds that there is no more a sense of safety than at the previous rung. But, instead of going back or assuming that the pursuit of performance is futile, the controller will often press on to a higher performance level, hoping that the next rung will provide the sense of security, safety, and lack of anxiety that is sought. To me, this video of yours, Dr. K., is all about performancedriven individuals. These individuals often have a terrible sense of self identity, and sometimes will cope with it by simply being down and depressed. But many of these individuals learn a reactive mechanism in life, which is that When I perform well, other people like that, and they acknowledgepraisenotice me. That is certainly better than feeling bad about myself. What if I just become the person who performs really well with everything I do? Wouldn't that guarantee that people like me, since I would always be performing well? I then watch these individuals go on to burn themselves out with the neverending performative lifestyle. I wish for these people to heal and do better for themselves. It really is painful when you get caught in the trap of trying to perform your way out of your bad sense of identity into a good one. And it sucks even more when you realize that your performances in life have not built a new, better identity but instead have amounted to no more than a false, pseudoidentity that really is not who you are deep down. text: I'm not doctor K., or a psychiatrist, but I'm in a similar field visual artist and have dealt with the same thing. I think the answer is measuring what you can sustainably do in the long run to achieve your goal. What doctor K. said at the end was really helpful, you have to find that baseline happiness or something like worklife balance, or in this case, effort and mental balance. Practice and working hard usually suck. If you have really ambitious goals having to work hard is probably not something that can be avoided. But by accepting the you of right now the stress and pressure of performance might go down, which makes that sort of concentrated effort easier. If you don't have your ego riding on whether you're a grindset kinda guy then you'll 1 have less stress around the task 2 will be able to avoid longterm burnout and constant quitting because you'll be able to recognize your limits better or when you might need a break, instead of pushing through. By deattaching from the highs and lows and just learning to take it day by day and not putting such high emotional stakes you can keep on practicing for a longer span of time. The ego also causes us to make up deadlines I want to be better than this person in x amount of time, or 'my music should sound like y soon or I've failed'. What we're trying to do is make the goods and bads matter less. You might also not like what you find out, maybe you can only handle 3 hours of making music a week before you feel miserable. Then you either have to find a way to be less miserable what that looks like could be different, maybe it's making music with friends, or maybe you reward yourself with something, or try and poke at what's causing the misery and try and lessen it etc or you'll have to accept that that's the pace you'll be going at, and it might take you a while longer, but you'll still be doing what you care for and improving.

text: Allowing all emotions is only the first step. The next step is disidentifying with them and especially the narratives behind them. You are not your emotions, and the stories your mind tells you about why you feel them are not reality. They may be justifiable, but they tend to keep you trapped in victim mentality powerlessness I have the right to feel this way because these things happened to me I have the right to continue poisoning myself with toxic emotions and never resolve and heal these wounds. You certainly have the right to feel the way you feel, but you also have the right to move past and heal those feelings. Many instead tend to stay stuck in those feelings and narratives. The mind naturally seeks to understand and interpret everything, so it creates deluded narratives or one small slice of truth that excludes many other piecesperspectives of the puzzle behind your emotions, especially where others are wrong and we are the victims. This isn't to say there aren't innocent victims of horrible things, but this mentality is not helpful for ourselves as it keeps us powerless to a past we did not choose and cannot change. Telling yourself more positive, empowering stories doesn't ultimately help either. It may feel a bit better, but it's just bandaging the wounds with new, bettersounding stories. And the wounds beneath the bandages remain unhealed. This is where people end up resigning themselves to, I've just come to accept that I'm always going to have these wounds deep down. But at least I acknowledge them and can function in spite of them now! So the next step is to detach yourself from the emotions. You are not your emotions you are that which is aware of these emotions. They are merely trapped energies that had not been allowed to pass through you at the time of trauma and therefore became samskaras. Observe them, allow them, feel them, and then detach from identifying with them to allow them to dissolve. This isn't suppression nor bypassing on the contrary, you are completely allowing them to arise and be fully felt. You are just not identifying with them. Instead of I am angry or I am sad it is, there is anger arising or there is sadness arising. Or even better, there are sensationstrapped energiesarising to be released. This too shall pass. When you say, I am sad, you become the sadness. And as long as you are your emotions, they will never dissolvebecause they have become a part of you, and you cannot dissolve that which you are. Detach yourself from the narratives. The stories the mind tells you about why you are feeling these emotions are just stories delusions, or one very small part of a story with infinite components. You are not the narrator, you are not the mind. As Dr. K said, you are not even the one to whom these things happened. The you now is actually a completely different youdifferent cells, different neurons, etc. Yet you still carry the stories as heavily as if it they are still you. As if the victimizationtrauma that happened 1020 years ago is still happening to you now. To take this one step further, you are not even the person who is here now you are that which is aware of the person, the mind, the emotions, the sense perceptions, the stories the awareness itself. The mind talks, but notice that it isn't you. If it was you, you should be able to make it stop whenever you want or think only the kinds of thoughts you want it to think. But you can't. Instead you often find yourself gripped with incessant negative, unhelpful thoughts that drive you mad and make you feel much worse. It's a CPU on autopilot. And what it says, no matter how convincing, isn't ultimately true. Allow it to say what it wants, but don't identify with or believe the stories. Don't follow them down their imaginary rabbit holes. You don't have to suppress the thoughts or replace them with positive thoughts. Instead, rather than allowing your attention to be caught up in the stories of the mind, bring your attention instead to the sensations in the body i.e. emotions and focus on fully allowing and feeling the sensations without the stories. When thoughts arise, go deeper into the sensations. Examine them more closely. Where exactly do you feel the sensations? Relax and allow it. Notice how it is constantly moving and changing. Examine them deeper and continue to allow them to fully arise, fully be felt, and relax, allowing them to move and change as they want to they will naturally dissolve if allowed to run their full, natural, uninhibited course in this way. And the more precisely you examine sense perceptions or emotions if using listening, for example, listen for the quietest sound you can hear birds in the distance, etc, as this requires more attention than listening for loud, general sounds, the more focused the mind becomes and the thinking slows or stops. The mind cannot both carefully examine or focus on sensations while also thinking. You can also start with focusing on the breath, breathing slowly in and out, then when the mind gets bored of this, pay attention to sense perceptions andor emotions, one at a time. But remember to continue to relax, so the energy can flow freely. Tension traps energy. As long as you believe in the stories your mind tells you, the emotions will always remain, because their existence will be justified. Poor me, I am a victim of abuse and therefore carry these traumas. Everytime you tell yourself these stories, the emotions get reinforced. And they will justifiably be a part of you. This is who I am and I am justified in being this way due to these stories. This is true of the personthe person is who they are due to circumstances beyond their control past, environment, genetics. But the person isn't you. As long as you believe yourself to be the person with its past stories and emotions, you will never transcend thembecause you are completely identified with them me the victim, etc. And once again, you cannot dissolve that which you are. You must detach from these and see they are merely words and sensations appearing in consciousness. And you are the consciousness in which they appear, and the awareness of them. From personal experience, doing this over and over has allowed me to dissolve most if not all traumas from childhood and throughout my life and most negative emotions permanently, such that I am no longer able to feel such emotions anymore, even if I try to. This is how you completely, permanently dissolve negative emotions, thoughts, old habit patterns, and samskaras and become free from them. Many spiritual teachers teach this technique, and if you are interested, I would highly recommend Michael Singer's The Untethered Soul, as he covers this method very well and in depth. The audiobook I find to be particularly helpful to be able to practice the techniques while listening simultaneously, and you can even find it free on youtube. Best wishes to you on your journey however it may go

text: The biggest problem I've seen is the constant disconnect between budgetexpectations and the work itself. People at the top or product managers, for example, often do not even understand the scope of work on a macro level. An easy way to spot this is when determining the age old question of, How long will this take? The devs say 23 weeks. The manager says, Ok, let's do it in 4 days and we need a POC by Friday morning. This arbitrary goalpost then forces the devs to work overtime, usually without pay, and in overdrive mode, to try and meet this deadline. The code quality is worse, the bugs are everywhere, but we can move fast and break things. If things fail, who gets blamed, do you think? Good code is almost never the goal because it isn't realistically attainable with these undervalued restraints. This toxic viewpoint is in almost every dev environment I've ever been in, even in the good companies I've worked for. It's a lack of respect for the work and the actual ability of these very talented people and I wish it would stop, but there is no incentive for it to. Too many people, much similar to artists, are eager to prove themselves and even for free if need be do I even bother bringing up the entire slave internship dilemma?. Then you have open source. A beautiful construct of community work and innovation, which is, of course, exploited once again and further contributes to this perception. Entire swathes of companies and corporations are built on someone else's free software. I love what I do and the challenge, and honestly most devs I know got in it for the same reasons. This passion is often what gives us an unnatural resilience, but it also creates a serious mountain that is impossible for most thus the burnout. Luckily, I made it on top of my mountain, but I cannot fathom being a junior or even just starting out in this climate, especially with the ascent of AI. The next generation will only get it even worse unless something significant changes. The market will not fix this problem because it does not want the best product, it wants the cheapest. So potentially some policy protections from government or similar might be the only way an external force can change the trend of how this is handled.

text: There's a multitude of reasons but I'll write two of them, they aren't applicable to everyone but many at least. 1. Sprints. It's a good idea, split things into smaller portions so you can get things done faster and judge progress easier. The problem is that it's literally like a sprint, but instead of it being a short spurt, you're now forced to run at that speed for an ultramarathon. 2. Work load and deadlines. If you're good at your job you'll get increasingly more demanding work assigned to you, you'll have responsibility for more things and the more you succeed, the worse it gets. You'll have shorter deadlines, you'll get assigned a task with a deadline, then you'll in the middle of that get assigned something else with a tighter deadline and now you're essentially expected to do twice the work in the same amount of time when the deadline was already tight. Then you're blamed for not succeeding because you succeeded a previous time. The two are very similar in nature and essentially make the job place more and more straws on the camel's back until it can no longer stand. It's awful.

text: It's funny. I burned out on exercise and training, figured out I was pushing myself too hard. I got an education in IT and became a dev. At the interview I was told that I would work with legacy and renewing it. I knew this was a very unpopular type of work, but I just wanted to get into the field. Idk what happened mentally, but the second I secured the job, I immediately checked out of responsibility. I worked far less than I'm required to do, but my company is actually pretty cool with it. And I accepted the fact that I would suck for several years. This last one is important, because many feel a lot of pressure to be really awesome when they are a beginner. When you're new to something, anything, you will suck regardless. So just embrace it. I'm going to be trash at this for the next 5 years, but in 23 years I'll be ok. Here's what I learned from my training. I was doing Japanese martial arts, which I think is important. A part of the traditional training is to push you past a breaking point. And then you do it again and again. Although it will fuck you up, the idea is to develop a mindset where you can get past adversity with flying colors. And ironically, when pushed to the edge a hundred times over, you learn that you have to be smart. You can't push your body and mind past the breaking point without breaking. If we look to the ancient writings of the most legendary sword masters, they don't talk about technique. It's all about the mind. And when I read Japanese history, the strategy during war was to always fight the easiest battle. Because winning was the goal. So I have an old document that says that you should never battle a spear master with a spear. You shoot him with a bow. In other words, never fight on the enemy's terms. You set your own terms. Taking this back to the modern world, your goals are most likely at odds with your employer. Their ultimate goal is highly experienced employees who work 247 with no pay. Your ultimate goal is probably to just do whatever the fuck you want and have some means of supporting that life. As long as you provide just enough for them to value your labor over looking for someone else, you should do the absolute minimum unless you enjoy it and want to do more. Focus on whatever are your personal goals and do what it takes. Don't be spellbound by the bullshit. They want you to think you need to be a top performer, but the truth is that they'll take almost anyone. And if they don't, someone else definitely wants you. So do battle on your own terms.

text: Another secret is to understand the cycle. The way development happen is that someone in the company promises the customer some sort of feature within some sort of deadline. This feature and deadline is 100 based on hooking the customer. It's not rooted in reality at all. That means it's not your deadline. You deliver by whatever deadline is comfortable for you, and they will HAVE TO adjust. If you're breaking your back to meet whatever delusional deadline they give you, they'll keep giving you unrealistic deadlines. If you're able to hit that deadline, they will push that envelope. So you should always fail to meet that deadline, bit by bit. If you're new, you shouldn't worry about failing to hit the deadline by a lot. Your bosses are likely experienced, and expect you to fail. So meet those expectations. The second most important part of understanding the cycle is that the second you finish a project, the next project starts. So why are you trying to hit the deadline if there's no difference from before and after? Maybe you get a piece of cake or a pizza, but you're right back at it. That means you shouldn't care about the deadline at all. That's your manager's responsibility. If he fucks it up, it's his fault. I've directly told one of the highest up that he's the one who has to answer the customer when we can't meet the deadline he arbitrarily set, knowing that we might not meet it. Seeing the blood drain from his face told me he was trying to pass the buck, and didn't expect to get caught. They know very well what they're trying to do, so don't accept it. text: Why It Sucks to Be a Software Developer Introduction Software development is one of the most coveted and competitive jobs Developers at FAANG companies can make base salaries over 1 million annually Yet developers have one of the highest suicide rates among professions 83 of developers experience burnout according to UK study In 2021, 20 of developers worldwide were looking for new jobs the Great Resignation The Core Problem Set Up to Fail Developers are uniquely positioned to be set up to fail and then blamed for failure Even success can lead to negative consequences Constantly Changing Expectations Developers have scopes of work and timelines like other professions Unlike other professions, these scopes and timelines change frequently Example CEOs who suddenly want to implement AI after listening to a podcast Timelines get cut in half or new features are demanded close to deadlines Blame Game When delivery fails, developers take the blame, not leadership No one blames the CEO who changed requirements 6 weeks before launch Pressure rolls downhill to developers The Success Trap When developers succeed despite impossible demands working weekends, overtime Instead of recognition, expectations are permanently raised Creates cumulative stress environment where stress piles up over time The Two Types of Developers Those who work extremely hard but don't get promoted and take blame for failures Those who work less but somehow get promoted and take credit This difference often comes down to soft skills and boundarysetting abilities Fundamental Mismatches in Software Development Mismatch Between Work Type and Environment Coding requires deep cognitive intensive focus But developers are rarely given uninterrupted blocks of time Expected to be available on SlackTeams, respond to messages, attend meetings Unlike doctors who aren't expected to answer emails during emergency room shifts Remote Work Paradox Remote work offers benefits no commute, flexibility But creates isolation and loneliness Blurs boundaries between work and home Difficult to establish when work actually ends Interpersonal Environment Issues Software development often selects for people with lower EQ and empathy Leads to harsh feedback, lack of credit, and poor management Creates a Darkest Dungeon effect where developers get increasingly beaten down Stress is cumulative without recovery periods The MBA Circle Jerk Technical people do the actual work while MBAs take the credit Management holds meetings all day that they want developers to attend When burnout happens, solutions are superficial mindfulness app subscriptions Developers need to learn some of those MBA circle jerk skills to succeed Unhealthy Coping Mechanisms Poor Stress Sensing Developers often don't recognize signs of stress headaches, muscle tightness, sleep issues Instead of addressing stress directly, they try to eliminate the source The Zerg Down Strategy When stressed about a task, developers try to eliminate it by working harder Analogous to video game strategy of attacking enemies without healing This approach fails longterm because there's no recovery period The cycle continues with new tasks immediately following completion Task Replacement When overwhelmed, developers procrastinate on difficult tasks Replace important work with easier, less important tasks Still working but avoiding the main source of stress Creates dot damage as the main project still looms Solutions Learn to Sense Stress Recognize physical and mental signs of burnout Address problems directly instead of grinding through Spend a turn healing yourself rather than just attacking the task Utilize Company Resources Research shows that familiarity with employee handbook and HR resources separates happy and unhappy developers Many companies have valuable resources that developers aren't aware of Employee Assistance Programs EAPs can provide significant help HR can often be an ally rather than an adversary Be Cautious of Wellness Theater Some company wellness initiatives are designed to extract more productivity Examples include meditation apps without addressing root causes Some companies use monitoring technology under the guise of wellness Key Actions and Observations Key Actions 1. Learn to recognize your stress signals before they become overwhelming 2. Address stress directly rather than just eliminating the source 3. Read your employee handbook and explore available resources 4. Speak with HR about support options for burnout prevention 5. Establish clear boundaries between work and personal time 6. Develop MBA circle jerk skills to advocate for yourself effectively 7. Take recovery time after intense work periods 8. Educate yourself through selfhelp resources and videos Key Observations 1. Software development creates a uniquely stressful environment due to changing expectations 2. Success often leads to higher expectations rather than recognition 3. The combination of cognitive intensive work with constant interruptions is fundamentally mismatched 4. Remote work offers benefits but creates new challenges for worklife balance 5. Software development environments often lack empathy and emotional intelligence 6. Developers' typical response to stress working harder creates a cumulative stress cycle 7. Company resources exist but are often underutilized by developers 8. The difference between thriving and burning out often comes down to soft skills and selfcare

text: A few lifehacks from a senior dev, 10y exp, having burnt out twice in my career before. Slack off from day 1, do the bare minimum at the longest pace you can. They're definitely going to fire me isn't a thing until you've had a 11 talk or a few with your direct manager about your poor performance. Until then, they're fine with your pace. Find a company that's going to be fine with your slacker pace. This is important, because you can have more personal time while also finishing your job on time as is fine with them. Crunching also becomes more rewarding and easier to plan, e.g. you can have an entire day off after the daily calls and then crunch 23 tasks the next day. This changes everything and reduces the stress drastically. Violate schedules, don't show up to useless meetings. This one is also about pushing the limits of slacking. Make it the norm for them to accept you not coming to a meeting provided it actually is pointless to you. You can say things like I don't have any more questions regarding this topic, so I'll skip the meeting or I'll watch the recording at another time to absorb the information, etc. You can use work as an excuse too, I really want to focus on this task instead, etc. If you manage to do it, this will alleviate a lot of stress. Actually read the handbook to see how much time you have to respond to chat messages and emails. Usually chat messages are limited to 46h within the work hours and emails are limited to 1 business day. Use it to your advantage. Listen to your feelings when hearing the messageemail notification and ask yourself, am I stable enough mentally right now to take a look at this message? If not, leave it for much later. If it's in the handbook, you're allowed to do this. Aint no way there's a company that will allow me to do all of this you'd be surprised. It may take a year or more of job hopping to actually find a company like this, but they do exist. Consider a lower paycheck too, because it's the money worth sacrificing for your own well being. And if you have a spouse, a kid, etc, then it's the money that will be sacrificed for their sake too. Currently you can't pay 10ky to be able to spend 15h a week more with your family, but you can make it a reality.

text: Software dev for 30 years now. This is an exaggeration, especially the 1m base salaries. Sure all of these things do exist to varying degrees, but healthy companies with good management do not have anywhere near the severity this video suggests. Better companies I've been at have been quite enjoyable to work at, with bosses and management that are much more realistic. I've had companies where I only came into work 1 day a week and schedule all meetings on Wednesdays in the office and all the other days are for nonmeeting work and remote. I've also have been able to push back against unrealistic expectations. 1 useful strategy is management gives you a scope of work and you respond with probabilities of different time scales 25 chance it can be done in a week, 90 chance in 3 weeks. Let them decide from there. The constantly shifting scope is a real thing, and it will always happen because that's the nature of software it's unrealistic to think you can fight it or avoid it. What you can do though is ask, what's the priority, do you want me to stop working on this other thing, it will be pushed backed if we do, is this higher priority or do you want me to finish out what I started first? Your job as an engineer is to give the facts to help management make the decisions, if you're not doing that and just agreeing to unrealistic expectations and then repeatedly failing to deliver, that doesn't serve you or the company. An additional problem with dev work is technical debt, as features pile on under deadlines, the quality of the codebase degrades and future features take longer to build and there are higher chances of defects due to building on a less than ideal foundation of code. Again, this is your responsibility to educate management, hey, we need some time to refactor this part of the code, if we do spend time here, we will be able to move faster in the future and defects will decrease, these are the areas that need it the most. Good management will understand this and budget for it. Again, your job is to ultimately help the company achieve its goals. By default, management is going to be under pressure to constantly deliver features and they will never let up, but ultimately your job is to present the facts. If refactoring means delivering no features for a few weeks but longer term you can deliver faster and with less defects, why wouldn't the company want that? Management is not your adversary, they are your ally and your job is to help them succeed at their job, and ultimately the company. Good management will balance all the factors and get you what you need if they can. In the beginning of your career or new company you might not have much pull, but as you deliver you will get more and more trust and support. Provide value and you will be given flexibility to work how you want. That being said, I've been at horrible companies as well, everything from I don't want to see any bugs, if there are any you're fired, to chairs being thrown across the office, to being yelled at you're fired in front of everyone, but knowing it wasn't official and then just ignoring it and continuing working and next day it's back to normal lol. text: Dev work is hard even without frequent changes to feature requirements and timeline. Software development is research work where you spend a lot o time exploring dead end ideas before you actually figure out a solution that works for your problem. But it's often managed like factory work where doing X hours of work will reliably produce Y amount of overall progress. The term sprint comes from the Agile work methodology which was intended to bring some more sanity to the process. The short summary is that work needs to be divided into small chunks that can be implemented in two weeks the sprint and management keeps close track of progress after each sprint, with customers getting regular product prototypes to test already implemented features. When development inevitably falls behind schedule, management is supposed to ask customers to choose from 3 options 1 Extend the deadline, 2 cut unimplemented features or 3 increase budget to add more developers. But what many software companies today call Agile is a cargo cult where developers are expected to magically meet the original feature requirements on time and within budget thanks to doing a bunch of weird meetings.

text: As a senior developer. I burned out early, I worked parttime and was doing a MSc. in Software Engineering at the same time. Here's some tips Do not, under any circumstance, respond to work emails, textmessages, or any messagingapp messages, outside of working hours. Meet up with your friends. Really, a social life is important. Workout. If you can move around easily, everything else will seem easier too. Automate everything. Every menial task you can think off, automate it. It's those tasks that slow you down and irritate. Use TDD. seriously, do it, it decreases cognitive load because you no longer have to think about everything your unit under test touches. Create short feedbackloops. Short feedback loops allow you to course correct long before a deadline. Address your techdebt even if your Product Owner prioritizes other work. If you don't it will stick in the back of your mind forever and you'll work around it. Measure everything. If you don't measure, you will end up perpetually discussing about costbenefits. Use measurements as a guide for decisions. I.e. use DevOps Research and Assessment DORA Capabilities as a guideline for your CICD. One of their core expected outcomes is wellbeing. text: I've been a software developer for over 10 years and worked at several companies. A lot of the points brought up here I have never experienced. Maybe it's a US vs. UK approach to work or just where I've worked but I doubt it. The point about working super late and on weekends isn't something I've seen. Most mature companies and managers know that the valuable employees, those who have been there a long time and accrued knowledge, can easily get a job elsewhere so burning them out is a bad long term plan. Most people I've worked with technical and non technical know that problems arise and that things can slip past the estimates, it's not a blame game and people know that software developers are doing their best. I've also not seen the narcissistic boss thing either, they know that if software developers say something isn't feasible within a certain amount of time, pushing people harder doesn't make features appear out of thin air. Here's what I think the real cause is there's no time for general maintenance. Most other engineering disciplines have standards and safety procedures that are set, offices are usually cleaned regularly and other routine tasks are handled by other people. In software development, the demands are featurefeaturefeaturebugfixmeetingsfeatures and no alloted time for maintenance. On the outside it's new features but under the hood we're building on top of things that need to be cleaned up, dumping more code in is so horrible. Imagine a kitchen where cooks pump out meals but it's never cleaned, would you look forward to going back to work the next day? Probably not. You have to either clean up without anyone noticing or really pushing for more time to do it. Software development is misunderstood by a lot of people, it is both technical and creative. We start with learning the basics and having a good technical foundation, eventually moving on to using the knowledge to build something with whatever approach you choose. The combination of both of those is very satisfying but it demands long periods of uninterrupted time an hour at least and there's always someone who wants an answer to a mundane question right away. That is one of the things that really bothers me the most, it may be different for others.

text: Actually, it is quite rational to take on other solvable tasks or as you say active challenges even though on the surface counterintuitive. When depressed, the mind is trying to save energy. The quickest shortcut is the classic overgeneralization fallacy. I can't solve these problems therefore I can't solve any problems which of course is a nonsequitur. A mentally exhausted or overwhelmed mind shifts from some to all to simplify its thinking. But it is that very fallacy that causes the problem. It is not a rational thought but the brain's fuel tank is so low so to speak that it can't fathom more than that. Starting with a simple easily solvable task demonstrates empirically to the rational mind that the conclusion is false and that nothing can be done.

text: I've found the opposite to be true. If I increase my number of active challenges and actually do them otherwise it's just more stuff I haven't done, then I end up with less time and energy for the passive challenges. Things that slip over to the next day multiple times, then it's a few weeks of months later when I get back to them and then they're a bigger challenge and things get worse. Here are two things I've done to feel less overwhelmed in general. Firstly, turning passive challenges into active challenges. This sounds weird and possibly something that you can't really do at first, so here's an example turning billsexpenses coming at you into I want to be financially organised. Having a bill come in and being stressed about it and it feeling like my money is being drained away is a nasty feeling. However, having a good idea of what my incomes and outgoings are means that bills are an expected part of a system I have mapped out and there are very few surprises a.k.a. things out of my control. The second thing has been to take any task I have to do that feels insurmountable and break it into several chunks that can be done independently. Any task that can be done in one action isn't the kind to make me feel overwhelmed, it's usually a multi step process with a moderatehigh amount of uncertainty. Let's take another example, I want my home to be clean and tidy. Doing that in one go is overwhelming and realistically will result in failure. However, if I break it down into tidyingcleaningdustingetc. and do it per room, each chunk is much more manageable. Sure, I've now got a lot more things to do, but individually they're not that scary and I can do a small bit each day to progress it. It requires being consistent and trusting the process, but making a problem a little bit smaller each time really helps. Again there's an aspect of passive active here, as I've redefined the problem into something that's my choice and I'm now in control of how that gets done.

text: Feeling overwhelmed can be successfully dealt with by understanding the relationship between passive and active challenges. Passive challenges are difficulties imposed on us, while active challenges are ones we choose to take on. Feeling overwhelmed occurs when passive challenges outweigh active challenges. Increasing the number of active challenges can help combat overwhelm. The principle of increasing active challenges applies not only to eating disorders but also to treatments for depression. Behavioral activation, taking on small challenges, can help gain control of life and alleviate depression. Taking control of unrelated challenges can help change our mindset and feel confident in tackling overwhelming problems. Unplugging or disarming the feeling of overwhelm is achieved by increasing active challenges and shifting the cognitive equation.
